messages.subject: Manual Weights to akde function
messages.body_plain:
Hello all!

I am attempting to submit manual weights to the akde function. A few months ago I was able to use this functionality ok but, after taking a few months break from my code, it seems like akde is no longer using the vector of weights supplied and just providing each observation with equal weight. Has anyone else had this issue/have advice for how to get around it? Below is a bit of my code that was functional in May. Telem_all_ds is a list of telemetry object where each individual has a telemetry object in the list. The script is working but when I pull the weights used they are all the same value.

kde_all_ds <-
  names(telem_all_ds) %>%
  set_names() %>%
  map(
    ~ akde(
      telem_all_ds[[.x]],
      SP = land_sp,

      # Locations expected to be outside of the polygon:

      SP.in = FALSE,

      # Don't include auto-correlation:

      CTMM = iid_all_ds[[.x]],

      # Include manual weights:

      weights = points_for_telem %>%
        filter(id == .x) %>%

        # Break into telemetry groups:

        split(f = .$individual.local.identifier) %>%
        map(
          ~.x %>%
            pluck("weights") %>%

            # Standardize the values so they sum to 1:
            { . / sum(., na.rm = TRUE) }
        )
    )
  )

Thanks for the help!
Annika

messages.subject: rsf.fit vs rsf.select
messages.body_plain:
Hi community,

I'm hoping to get some clarity here, and let me preface by saying I have zero experience with RSFs - never even learned about them in classes.

I have a group of white-tailed deer that I'm running RSFs for by biological season (fawning, rearing, rut, etc.).

I've been able to identify all habitat types present in their home ranges (10 total). I'm seeking some fine-resolution answers, which is why I haven't reclassified into fewer habitat types, but I don't love this number and will reclassify if recommended. I think I saw on here somewhere that anything more than 4 (or 6?) is pushing it.

After gleaning what I could from this user group and other resources, I've tried running rsf.select on a subset of deer individually. I've then fed the top model's formula into rsf.fit (again, for each individual).

I've done rsf.select because it sounds like that's what's best for multiple habitat types.

Am I on the right track? For some reason I have a weird feeling about what I'm doing. Any advice would be appreciated!

Sincerely,
Laura (PhD Candidate)

messages.subject: Re: [ctmm-user] rsf.fit vs rsf.select
messages.body_plain:
Hi Laura,

We advise always using rsf.select() because we have found that poorly estimated coefficients can cause problems when estimating population-level averages. This often happens, for example, when a specific cover type is not in an animal's home range, or occurs very rarely. No need for a secondary rsf.fit() command.

When using cover type data, remember that the coefficients are in comparison to a reference category (i.e., whatever cover type(s) is/are left out). A positive number is not selection for that coefficient--it is selection compared to the baseline reference category. I generally advise that folks make sure their reference category is relatively large (i.e., contains > 25% or so of an animal's locations, which ensures that selection for the reference category is well-estimated) and is visited roughly in proportion to availability (i.e., the proportion of locations in that cover type is roughly equal to the proportion that occurs in the home range or study area, which makes selection coefficients a little easier to interpret). I usually include very rare cover types (<2% of the landscape) in the reference category unless there is a priori reason to think they are biologically important, if exploratory analysis indicates that the animals really seem to seek them out, or if I am working with very large numbers of locations per animal that ensure that I have enough statistical power to detect biologically meaningful patterns of selection.

Jesse

messages.subject: Re: [ctmm-user] rsf.fit vs rsf.select
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jesse,

Thank you so much for your swift response!

I have indeed struggled with my understanding of the correct usage of cover types. For the sake of processing speed, I did end up reclassifying some habitats so that now I have 3 categories (1 raster for each category). Each raster contains 1s for the habitat of choice and 0 for everything else. And, all three rasters were created from the same original so that extent, resolution, etc. are identical. I don't think they are colinear - there are 0s that account for other habitat types that I chose not to include in any category. But, I guess I'm still lost because I don't have a reference category (unless it was auto referencing by alphabetical order?). As a reference category, you suggested a rare cover type that may not be biologically meaningful, but also rather large? I don't think I interpreted that correctly.

My categories right now are mixed hardwoods, coniferous, and mesic flatwoods. Mesic flatwoods are pretty evenly distributed and captured in the home ranges, and I don't have reason to believe they are especially meaningful. They are a nice middle ground, so to speak. Could I use mesic flatwoods as the reference group? Or, would the cover types I didn't categorize be better as the reference group?

I could scrap all this and simply evaluate wet habitats versus dry habitats, since I'm hypothesizing that females avoid swamps during fawning but select for them during rut. If I went with this route, what would that mean for my reference category?

A couple of other random questions - I had one individual that bucked everything but the null model (next model was like 67 away). What does that mean?

Lastly, I had yet another individual who's betas were all negative. I think I did something wrong here, but I saw somewhere that all negatives could be indicative of an animal really hunkering down. This was during fawning season and I wondered if that could be the reason. But again, I think I was off base somehow.

Thanks again!
Laura

messages.subject: Updated ctmmlearn materials
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm happy to share that we have updated `ctmmlearn`, the learning materials for `ctmm`, to include vignettes for many of the types of analyses currently available in the package, as well as a working glossary of terms. The vignettes are provided as R Markdown files, knitted HTML files, and corresponding R scripts, which walk through analyses using example datasets. All materials can be found in the `ctmmlearn` GitHub repository: https://github.com/ctmm-initiative/ctmmlearn

I hope that this can be a helpful resource for everyone!

Best,
Erika

messages.subject: Correlation between RSF covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I have what might be a bit of a broad question. I'm running rsf's using different land cover classes, and I'm concerned about possible spatial correlation between classes and its impact on the reliability of my rsf results. My understanding is that in traditional rsf's that use logistic regression, high spatial correlation between land cover classes (for example, classes of wetland) would make the final selection coefficients somewhat unreliable. I'm having difficulty understanding, however, if this is the case in ctmm's rsf functions, given that they use a point process model. My rsf results suggest strong selection for forested wetland, but strong selection against emergent and scrub/shrub wetland. Yet when I used Ripley's K to test for clustering among wetland classes, all 3 appeared to be spatially correlated. Would this clustering of wetlands invalidate the results of my rsf?

Apologies if this question is extremely basic or confusing, I struggle with the underlying statistics behind some parts of the ctmm package.

Thanks so much for your time!

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have segmented the above data in time and dael period. All data subsets suggest range residency - except for one individual (VPZ).

In VPZ, the premigration night/day variograms do not asymptote (see one variogram example below). However, that individual also has a significant data gap of ~1 week during that period - likely due to a device failure, battery etc. I do believe that the individual is range-resident, but the data gaps are creating the spike in svf and uncertainty.

Is my explanation plausible, and if it is, would it be valid to include the individual for ctmm model selection and assume range-residency? The segmentation was based on calendar dates for comparability between individuals, but perhaps I could segment around the data gap?

Any help would be greatly appreciated regarding possible next steps here.

Thank you!

messages.subject_clean: Trouble with outlie() using calibrated data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am getting this error message when trying to run the outlier function on calibrated data:

Error in x[SUB2] <- 4 * sqrt((x.SUB - 2)/(4 - x.SUB)) :
  NAs are not allowed in subscripted assignments
In addition: Warning message:
In dr > 0 & error > 0 :
  longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length

I do not have this problem when I use data that has not been calibrated.

I sifted through some previous conversation about this and I saw something about negative eigenvalues that could be producing the NAs - not sure if that's my case here. I've tried two functions (dplyr and base r) to convert NAs to zeros, but alas, it does not seem to make the NAs disappear (perhaps I'm embedding that function incorrectly?).

Any ideas?

Attaching my calibrated telemetry object. For context, I'm working with white-tailed deer in a dog hunt area, so it's important that I can identify outliers associated with chases. I also have an interesting phenomenon that I have not seen elsewhere in literature - multiple females making multiple excursions >1 km in every biological season (including seasons without dog hunting).

messages.body_plain:
Alrighty, I have figured out the problem. My calibration data included the collar's fix type (3D), but I had previously dropped that column from my movement data when I cleaned it several months ago. Therefore, when I calibrated the movement data, the final result included a 3D class and an "all" class that gave estimates of 0 and CIs of infinity. All I needed to do was add a 3D column to the original movement data and the problem was solved.

Cheers!

messages.subject: Re: RSF error
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stella,

I fixed rsf.select() on GitHub to not copy over NA coefficients from previous models.

I'd prefer not to get NA parameter estimates in the first place. So far, the only time I've seen this happen is when having too many categories in a categorical variable, so that there's no longer a functioning reference category being sampled. Outside of this, if you run into further issues, then I'd like to diagnose them, and you can feel free to send me a minimal working example to reproduce the issue.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: How to identify residency via SVF?
messages.subject_clean: How to identify residency via SVF?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Romain,

There's nothing new and no magic bullet at present. Things people have done and work okay include:
Applying a cutoff to DOF[area] - usually around 4-5 when the bias gets large
Applying a cutoff to the overlap between the home-range of the first and second halves of the data - usually around 90-95%
Applying a cutoff to tau[position] that make sense for your species.
There is also an internal function svf.test to rank the discrepancy between the empirical and theoretical variogram.

Best,
Chris
